name: Arabic
signature: Right-to-left, joined into one flowing cursive ribbon, with dots placed above and below the line.
combination: Written right-to-left and cursive: most letters JOIN their neighbours and change shape by position — isolated, initial, medial, final. Six letters (ا د ذ ر ز و) never connect to the letter that follows them, so they force a break. Short vowels are usually unwritten; when shown they are harakat (small marks) above or below. Many letters share one skeleton and differ only by the number and position of DOTS — so the dots are a real 'piece' to practise.
notes: Used by the Arabic track. The initial inventory below covers the greeting/self-introduction vocabulary; it grows toward the full 28-letter set. Stroke orders are the common handwriting convention (right-to-left), not a standard.

strokeOrderSource.variation: The page's Baa demonstration verifies the shared independent bowl from its upper-right tip continuously right-to-left to the turned-up left tip. The Taa demonstration opens on that complete bowl, places the left dot above at 00:00.45–00:00.70, then lifts again and places the right dot at 00:00.75–00:01.00. Because the Taa clip does not redraw the bowl, this learner path uses the separately demonstrated Arabic Baa body rather than inferring its direction from a still. The adjacent lesson identifies taa as a two-way connector and separately prints its contextual shapes. The path fits the course's vendored Noto Naskh outline; its Arabic provenance remains separate from the Persian record for the same Unicode glyph.

marks.attachesAs: fatḥa — a short slash ABOVE the consonant
kasra — a short slash BELOW the consonant
ḍamma — a small wāw-shape ABOVE the consonant
sukūn — a small circle ABOVE, marking no vowel
shadda — a small w-shape ABOVE, doubling the consonant
tanwīn fatḥ — double fatḥa, the indefinite '-an' ending (as in شكرًا)
